title.en: Pick the motion source that matches the requirement

summary: Choose authored clips, procedural functions or solved dynamics by what the motion must respond to, and keep one owner per transform.
objective: Select a motion model with the right responsiveness and correctness cost instead of defaulting to the most familiar one.
applies_when: A character, creature or mechanism must move and the technique has not been chosen.
Motion must react to user input, terrain, collisions or a physical parameter.
An existing animation needs to respond to something it was not authored for.
intent_signals: make it react when I push it
should it be physics or animation
example_prompts: The puppet should perform a scripted gesture but react when the user drags it.
Decide whether this creature needs physics or a hand-authored motion.
negative_signals: Static scenes and single camera moves.
Numerical simulations whose model is fixed by the subject rather than by expressive needs.
not_for: Static scenes and single camera moves.
Numerical simulations whose model is fixed by the subject rather than by expressive needs.

principles: Authored clips give exact artistic control and are inexpensive to evaluate, but they are not free: a mixer still advances clip time and updates the animated properties every frame. What a clip lacks is a dynamics solve, so it cannot avoid an obstacle, absorb an impact or respond to a changed mass.
Procedural motion, driven by time, parameters or a simple controller, responds continuously and stays cheap and predictable, at the cost of hand-crafted nuance.

Solved dynamics produces responses nobody authored, which is exactly the point when contact and momentum are the subject; the price is that the solver, not the artist, owns the transforms, and that direct pose writes fight it.
The important question is not which is most advanced but what the motion must answer to: a rehearsed performance, a continuous parameter, or a physical interaction.
implementation: Classify the motion first: rehearsed performance, parameter response, or physical consequence. Choose clip, procedural or solver accordingly, and record the choice with the artifact.
Mix by body part or by phase rather than per frame: an authored upper-body gesture over a procedural walk, or an authored fall that hands over to the solver at release.
Where a solver owns a body, drive it through forces, impulses or velocities; setting the transform directly is a teleport and is not a physically meaningful action.
Use kinematic bodies for objects that must follow an authored path but still push dynamic objects, and keep that distinction explicit in the scene description.
Give every moving transform exactly one owner at a time and make handovers explicit events.
observable_checks: Interact with the object in a way the author did not anticipate, such as pushing during a gesture; a clip-only actor ignores it entirely.
Look for the signature of a fight over ownership: jitter, interpenetration or objects snapping back to a path after a collision.

Choose a parameter change with a predicted consequence and compare the result against that prediction: apply the same impulse to bodies of different mass and check that the resulting speeds differ in the predicted ratio, or change the pair friction coefficient while a body is actually sliding on a contact. A null result from an undiscriminating test proves nothing, because ideal free-fall acceleration is independent of mass and an airborne or already resting body need not respond to a friction change.
Pause playback and confirm the actor holds a coherent pose rather than a blend artefact.
Trace which value the moving transform actually reads each frame: a clip track, a procedural expression or a solver pose. Ownership is the fact; the visual result can look identical either way.

creative_affordances: Hybrid pipelines are normal and welcome; the rule asks for explicit ownership, not purity.
A stylised, non-physical response can be the better artistic answer even where a solver was available.
known_limits: Authored selection guidance with one documented engine behaviour cited; no runtime comparison of techniques was performed.
Says nothing about which specific engine or library to install.

claims.statement: In Rapier, directly changing the position of a rigid body is equivalent to teleporting it, which is not a physically realistic action; forces, impulses or velocity changes are the recommended way to move dynamic bodies, while kinematic bodies are user-controlled and fixed bodies do not move.
claims.scope: Documented behaviour of one rigid-body engine; it describes control responsibilities, not the accuracy of any particular simulation.

source_refs.locator: Rigid-body types; position setting versus forces and impulses

claims.statement: A Three.js animation mixer is a player for animations on a particular object, and its update method advances the mixer time and updates the animation; it is normally called once per frame with the delta time from a clock or timer.
claims.scope: Documented playback behaviour of one animation system. It establishes that clip playback performs per-frame work, not that any particular scene is or is not simulated.
